0.title: Living Before the Wrong Audience
0.essay:
Someone questions your work in a meeting. A remark you made comes out wrong, and you see a face change. Later, alone, your stomach tightens. What do they think of me now? Will this follow me? Could it cost me my place, even my job? If you know that feeling, this study is for you.

A snare, not a weakness of character

The Bible has a name for this experience. “The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe” (Proverbs 29:25). A snare is a trap hidden in the grass. You do not see it until it has your foot. The fear of man is like that. It rarely feels like fear of people. It feels like being careful, being sensible, protecting your future. But it holds you fast, and it hurts.

You are not unusual. Prophets, kings and apostles were caught in this snare, as later chapters will show. It is not a sign that you are a poor Christian. It is a sign that your heart, like every heart, longs to be accepted, and has not yet fully rested that longing on God.

Where we are going

This study does not offer a technique for confidence. It offers something better: a God so great and a Saviour so kind that the opinions of others shrink to their proper size. We will look honestly at what happens in us when we feel challenged or misread, and why. Then we will hear God’s verdict in Christ, learn to fear him rather than people, look at Jesus, the one truly free man, and end with practical wisdom for the moment itself and the long evening afterwards.

The study The Fear of the Lord has a chapter on the fear of God and the fear of man, which this study builds on rather than repeats.

The chapters

The Snare Springs; What Lies Beneath; The Verdict That Ends the Trial; Fear God, and Nothing Else; Jesus, Who Was Free; and In the Moment and Afterwards.

For reflection

When did you last feel the fear of what someone thought of you? What did you most fear losing in that moment?

1.title: The Snare Springs
1.essay:
It can happen in a second. A colleague says, “I’m not sure that’s right.” A friend goes quiet after something you said. An email arrives with a curt tone. Your heart speeds up, your face grows warm, and a voice inside begins to argue your case.

What happens inside

In that moment it feels as if you are on trial. Not just your idea or your sentence, but you. A challenge to your work feels like a challenge to your worth. A misunderstanding feels like a verdict: they have seen the real you, and found you wanting. That is why it hurts so much. Something far bigger than one conversation seems to be at stake.

Then the courtroom moves indoors. Hours later you are still replaying the exchange. You rehearse what you should have said. You read meanings into a glance or a short reply. You imagine the worst: the manager talking about you, the reputation slipping, the job lost, the income gone, the family let down. One awkward moment becomes a whole future of disgrace. David knew that inner noise: “For I hear the whispering of many” (Psalm 31:13). Whether the whispering is real or imagined, it can keep a person awake all night.

This does not make you strange. It makes you a person who longs to be safe and accepted. But Scripture shows us where that longing can lead when it rests on the wrong thing.

The first hiding

The fear of being seen goes back to the garden. After Adam and Eve sinned, they sewed fig leaves together and hid among the trees. When God called, Adam said, “I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself” (Genesis 3:10). Ever since, human beings have been covering and hiding. We manage our image. We dread exposure. Underneath much of our fear of others is that old sense of nakedness: if they really saw me, they would not accept me.

Notice what God did. He came looking. “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9) was not the call of someone who wanted to shame Adam, but of someone who would not leave him hidden. Before the chapter ends, God himself clothes them.

A king, a priest and an apostle

King Saul was told to obey God fully, and did not. When Samuel confronted him, he admitted the reason: “I have sinned, for I have transgressed the commandment of the LORD and your words, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice” (1 Samuel 15:24). And even then his chief concern was his image: “yet honor me now before the elders of my people” (1 Samuel 15:30). Saul shows how the fear of man can rule a man with a crown on his head.

Aaron, left in charge while Moses was on the mountain, gave way to the crowd and made a golden calf. When Moses challenged him, Aaron blamed the people, “You know the people, that they are set on evil” (Exodus 32:22), and then told an almost comic story: “I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf” (Exodus 32:24). Feeling exposed, he reached for blame and excuses.

Peter had promised to die with Jesus. Hours later, in a courtyard, a servant girl said, “You also were with Jesus the Galilean” (Matthew 26:69). It was only a question from someone with no power at all, yet Peter denied it, then denied it with an oath. The fear of man does not need a powerful opponent. A raised eyebrow is enough. Years later Peter fell into the same trap at Antioch, drawing back from Gentile believers, “fearing the circumcision party” (Galatians 2:12).

Faith kept quiet

John tells us of leaders who believed in Jesus “but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue; for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God” (John 12:42–43). Being put out of the synagogue meant losing community, standing and often livelihood. These were not wicked men. They were frightened men with a great deal to lose. John names the root plainly: they loved one glory more than another.

An example

A nurse in her thirties is asked by a senior doctor, in front of the team, why a chart was not updated. She had in fact updated it, but the system had not saved it. She mumbles an apology she does not owe and spends the evening sure that everyone now thinks she is careless. By bedtime she has imagined a formal warning. The next morning nobody mentions it. The doctor has forgotten. She has not.

Not the end of the story

Every one of these portraits points beyond itself. Adam was clothed by God. Peter was met by the risen Jesus on a beach and restored, three times, by name. Where the snare has caught us, Christ comes looking too.

For reflection

What kinds of moments most often make you feel “on trial”? When you replay a conversation, what are you hoping to change, or to prove? Which of the portraits in this chapter is most like you: Adam hiding, Saul managing his image, Aaron making excuses, Peter denying, or the leaders keeping quiet? What does it mean to you that God came looking for Adam?

2.title: What Lies Beneath
2.essay:
The fear of man is not only a feeling. It is a sign. It shows what our hearts are leaning on. When we are terrified of losing someone’s approval, it is usually because, without realising it, we have been asking that approval to do for us what only God can do.

The glory we receive from one another

Jesus asked some religious leaders a searching question: “How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?” (John 5:44). Glory here means weight, honour, standing. Jesus says that when our sense of worth is supplied by other people, it becomes hard to trust him at all. We are already looking to another source.

Paul faced the same choice: “For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10). You cannot have two masters setting the terms of your worth. One will rule.

False saviours

The Bible calls anything we look to for life in place of God an idol. Idols are usually good things given a weight they cannot bear. Beneath the fear of man there are often several:

Approval. The need to be liked, thought well of, never disappointing anyone. Reputation. The need to be seen as competent, wise, reliable, never foolish. Status. The need to keep my place in the order of things, to be respected and not overlooked. Security. The need to know that my job, my income and my future are safe.

Each of these promises something like salvation: “If you have this, you will be all right.” So when it is threatened, it feels like being condemned. That is why a single critical comment can feel like the ground giving way. We have built on it.

Two faces of one fear

It is easy to think the fear of man belongs only to shy or insecure people. In fact it has two faces. One is insecurity: shrinking, apologising, avoiding conflict, saying what people want to hear. The other is pride: needing to win every argument, defending ourselves sharply, boasting, unable to admit a mistake. They look opposite, but they share a root. Both are focused on how I appear. Both need other people’s verdict to feel safe. The proud person needs to be admired; the insecure person dreads being despised. Both are, in different ways, still on trial.

Scripture’s answer to both is the same. It is not to think more highly of ourselves, nor to think worse of ourselves, but “to think with sober judgment” (Romans 12:3), and then to think about ourselves rather less. The study Humility & Pride explores this further.

Comparison feeds it

Much of our fear grows from measuring ourselves against others. Paul spoke of people who “measure themselves by one another and compare themselves with one another” and said they “are without understanding” (2 Corinthians 10:12). Comparison turns every colleague into a judge and every meeting into a scoreboard.

Good things in their place

None of this means that what people think does not matter. “A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches” (Proverbs 22:1). A reputation for honesty and kindness is a gift, and it helps our witness. Work and income matter too: they feed families and serve others, as the study Christian at Work shows.

The problem is not caring. It is caring ultimately. A good name is a good servant and a cruel master. When it is in its place, you can protect it calmly, correct a misunderstanding, and even lose it for a time without losing yourself. When it is on the throne, every threat to it is a threat to you.

Jesus even warned, “Woe to you, when all people speak well of you” (Luke 6:26). If everyone approves of us all the time, we are probably shaping ourselves to the crowd rather than to God. Some disapproval is simply the cost of living honestly.

An example

A man in middle management notices that he cannot let any comment about his department pass. He always has an answer, a reason, a story about why it was someone else’s fault. His wife says, gently, that he seems frightened. At first he is offended. Then he realises she is right. Underneath the confidence is a boy who grew up being told he would never amount to much. He has spent his whole life trying to prove that voice wrong.

Naming it is a mercy

To see this in ourselves can feel humiliating. But it is the beginning of freedom. “Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts!” (Psalm 139:23). God does not show us our idols to shame us, but to free us from masters that could never love us back.

For reflection

Which of the four, approval, reputation, status or security, has the strongest grip on you? Does your fear of man tend to look more like insecurity or more like pride? What would it look like to care about your good name without it ruling you? Pray Psalm 139:23–24 slowly, and listen.

3.title: The Verdict That Ends the Trial
3.essay:
If the fear of man is the feeling of always being on trial, the gospel is news that the trial is over. In Christ, the most important verdict about your life has already been given, and it is not “guilty”, nor “not good enough”. It is “accepted”.

No condemnation

Paul writes, “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Not less condemnation, or condemnation postponed. None. The reason is not that we have performed well, but that Christ has. “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). This is what the Reformers called justification by faith alone. God counts the believer righteous, not because of anything in us, but because of Christ’s perfect life and sacrificial death, received by faith.

The deepest question of your life is settled. You are not waiting to find out whether you measure up.

Who can bring a charge?

Romans 8 ends in a courtroom. “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31). Paul imagines accusers stepping forward, and answers each one. “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33). The judge himself has ruled in your favour. “Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died … who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us” (Romans 8:34).

Remember that the next time you are challenged or misread. Their opinion matters, and you may need to answer it, but it is not the final court. The final court has sat, and the one who sits at its right hand is praying for you.

Paul’s strange freedom

Some in Corinth were criticising Paul, comparing him unfavourably with other teachers. His answer is remarkable. “But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself. For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me” (1 Corinthians 4:3–4).

Paul does not say their opinion means nothing, only that it is a very small thing. And he does not even sit as judge over himself. He has stepped out of the courtroom altogether, both the outer court of other people and the inner court of his own conscience, because the Lord is the judge, and the Lord has already declared him righteous in Christ.

This brings a particular kind of freedom. Most of us live as if we must earn a verdict by our performance: do well, be liked, then feel secure. The gospel turns this round. The verdict comes first, and our work and relationships flow from it. A person who knows this is not forever thinking about how they are coming across. They are not thinking less of themselves so much as thinking of themselves less. Their attention is free to go outward, to the work, to the people in front of them, to God. This is self-forgetfulness, and it is restful.

Paul adds, “Then each one will receive his commendation from God” (1 Corinthians 4:5). The praise you crave from people is a faint echo of the commendation God will one day speak over his children. You do not have to grasp for it now.

Not only acquitted, but adopted

The gospel is not only a courtroom. It is a family. “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15). Paul links slavery and fear. A slave is always anxious about whether he has done enough. A child in a good home knows he belongs, even on a bad day.

“See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1). Those last four words are worth saying slowly. Your standing does not rise and fall with this week’s meetings. God has blessed you “in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6), which means that the Father’s delight in his Son now rests on you because you are joined to him.

Received, not achieved

Our culture tells us to build an identity by success and admiration. That identity is fragile: whatever we achieve can be lost, and whoever applauds can stop. The gospel gives an identity that is received, not achieved. It cannot be taken away by a hard question in a meeting, a misread message or even the loss of a job.

An example

A teacher dreads parents’ evenings, sure that every complaint proves she is failing. A friend asks her one day, “What does God say about you?” She has no quick answer. Over the following months she writes Romans 8:1 and 1 John 3:1 on a card in her bag. The complaints still come. But she finds she can listen to them as information rather than as a sentence on her life. Some she acts on; some she gently disagrees with.

For reflection

Whose verdict do you most often feel you are waiting for? How does Romans 8:31–34 answer the fear of being judged? What would it look like for you to think of yourself less, rather than worse or better? Say aloud 1 John 3:1, ending with “and so we are”. What changes if this is true?

4.title: Fear God, and Nothing Else
4.essay:
The cure for the fear of man is not to stop fearing altogether. It is to fear the right one. When God is great in our eyes, people take their true size: neither monsters nor gods, but fellow creatures to be loved.

Who are you to be afraid?

God spoke to his exiled people through Isaiah: “I, I am he who comforts you; who are you that you are afraid of man who dies, of the son of man who is made like grass, and have forgotten the LORD, your Maker, who stretched out the heavens and laid the foundations of the earth” (Isaiah 51:12–13).

Look at the order. First God says, “I am he who comforts you.” Only then does he ask the question. It is an invitation to see clearly. The manager whose opinion you dread, the colleague who challenged you, the friend who misread you: each is a person “who dies”, “made like grass”. They are real, and they matter, but they are small and passing. The fear of man always involves forgetting. We forget the Maker of the heavens and fill the sky with faces.

And then comes a question that is almost gentle humour: “And where is the wrath of the oppressor?” (Isaiah 51:13).

Sparrows and hairs

When Jesus sent out his disciples, he warned them plainly that they would be maligned. “If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more will they malign those of his household” (Matthew 10:25). He did not promise them a good reputation. He promised them something deeper.

“And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows” (Matthew 10:28–31).

Notice how quickly Jesus moves from the one we should fear to the Father who counts our hairs. The God who is to be feared is the same God who cares for you in the smallest detail. To fear him is not to live in terror. It is to live in reverent trust before a Father whose opinion of you is the one that counts, and whose care reaches further than anyone’s criticism.

What can man do to me?

Psalm 56 was written, its heading tells us, when the Philistines seized David in Gath. He was a fugitive, misunderstood and in danger. Yet he wrote, “You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle. Are they not in your book?” (Psalm 56:8). God notices the nights when we toss and turn over what someone said. “This I know, that God is for me” (Psalm 56:9). And the refrain rises: “in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can man do to me?” (Psalm 56:11).

Psalm 118 says it again: “The LORD is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me?” (Psalm 118:6). People can do quite a lot: misjudge us, gossip, dismiss us, even end our employment. But they cannot undo God’s love, cancel his verdict or remove us from his hand. What they can do is real but limited. What God has done is final.

Our name, our work and our bread

Much of our fear is about provision. If my reputation suffers, will I lose my job? If I lose my job, how will we live? Jesus speaks directly to this: “your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:32–33).

Psalm 37 speaks to those who feel wronged: “Commit your way to the LORD; trust in him, and he will act. He will bring forth your righteousness as the light, and your justice as the noonday” (Psalm 37:5–6). God cares about your name. He is able to vindicate you, sometimes in this life, and certainly on the last day.

Christians do sometimes lose jobs, are sometimes misjudged for years, and do sometimes face real hardship. Joseph was falsely accused and thrown into prison with his good name in ruins. Yet “the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love” (Genesis 39:21). God did not prevent the loss. He was present in it, and he was weaving it into a good purpose that Joseph could not yet see. Our hope is not that nothing bad will happen, but that nothing can separate us from our Father’s care.

An example

An engineer is made redundant after a restructuring, and wonders if a disagreement with his director played a part. For weeks he feels ashamed. His pastor reads Isaiah 51 with him and asks, “Who are you more afraid of, the director, or the God who made the heavens?” He still applies for jobs with an ache in his chest. But he begins to pray, “My name and my bread are in your hands.” Four months later he starts a new role.

For reflection

Who looms largest in your mind when you fear what others think? How does Isaiah 51:12–13 help you see them in their true size? What does Matthew 10:28–31 tell you about how God sees you? What fear about your work or provision do you need to commit to the Lord today?

5.title: Jesus, Who Was Free
5.essay:
There has been one human life entirely free from the fear of man. Jesus was misjudged, slandered and rejected, yet he was never ruled by what people thought. Yet he loved people more than anyone has ever loved them.

Not swayed by appearances

Even his enemies saw it. Trying to trap him, they came with flattery: “Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone’s opinion. For you are not swayed by appearances, but truly teach the way of God” (Mark 12:14). They meant it as a trap, but every word was true. Jesus did not shape his message to please the powerful or the crowd.

John tells us why. When many believed in him because of his signs, “Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people and needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man” (John 2:24–25).

Secure in his Father’s love

Where did it rest? At his baptism, before he had preached a sermon or healed anyone, the Father said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). Jesus lived from that delight, not towards it. “And he who sent me is with me. He has not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29).

That security made him free to serve. On the night he was betrayed, John says Jesus knew “that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going back to God” (John 13:3). And so he took a towel and washed his disciples’ feet. A person who is secure in God does not need to protect their dignity. They can kneel.

Misjudged and despised

Jesus knew what it is to be misread. When he ate with sinners, people said, “Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!” (Matthew 11:19). Religious leaders said he was in league with the devil. He was “despised and rejected by men … and as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not” (Isaiah 53:3).

At the cross his reputation was destroyed in public. He was stripped, mocked and paraded as a criminal. The chief priests jeered, “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Mark 15:31). Every fear we have of exposure, humiliation and loss of standing, he met in full.

And yet: “looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2). To despise the shame does not mean he did not feel it. It means he refused to let it decide what he would do. He counted it as nothing compared with the joy of saving his people. “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23).

Free to love

Jesus’ freedom from people did not make him indifferent to people. It made him able to love them truly. “When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them” (Matthew 9:36). When a rich young man came to him, “Jesus, looking at him, loved him” (Mark 10:21), and then told him a hard truth he did not want to hear. The people-pleaser cannot do that. The fear of man makes us use people to feel safe. The freedom Jesus had let him give himself away.

He bore our shame

Jesus is not only our example. He is our substitute. He bore not only our guilt but our shame. He was exposed so that we could be clothed. He was rejected by men and forsaken on the cross so that we could be welcomed by God. Because of him, “he is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11). The one whose opinion matters most is not ashamed of you.

And the promise of Isaiah becomes ours: “whoever believes in him will not be put to shame” (1 Peter 2:6). Not that we will never be embarrassed or misjudged, but that the final, lasting shame we fear has been carried away.

United to him

The New Testament says believers are joined to Christ. “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3). Your real life is not on display in the meeting room or the group chat. It is hidden, safe, with Christ. His standing with the Father is your standing. His Spirit lives in you, slowly making you like him: secure enough to stop performing, and free enough to love.

An example

A young pastor finds himself checking after every sermon whether people liked it. Reading Hebrews 12:2, he is struck that Jesus despised the shame for the joy set before him. He begins praying before he preaches, “Lord, you are not ashamed of me. Let me love these people, not need them.” He notices that he listens to people more after the service, instead of scanning their faces for approval.

For reflection

Which moment in Jesus’ life most moves you as you think about the fear of man? What does it mean that Jesus “despised the shame”? How does knowing he is “not ashamed to call them brothers” speak to your fears? How might security in Christ free you to love someone rather than need them?

6.title: In the Moment and Afterwards
6.essay:
The truths of the gospel are not only for quiet times. They are meant for the meeting, the awkward conversation and the long evening of replaying it. Here is some practical wisdom, offered not as a new set of rules to perform, but as ways to live out of the freedom Christ has already given.

In the moment: pause and pray

When you feel challenged, your body reacts first: a racing heart, a hot face. Take a breath before you answer. Nehemiah, asked a dangerous question by the king, records, “So I prayed to the God of heaven” (Nehemiah 2:4), and then he spoke. A silent prayer of a few words is enough: “Father, you are here. I am yours.” This is a conversation, not a verdict.

Answer honestly and calmly

“Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger” (James 1:19). Listen to the challenge properly. Is there something true in it? If so, you can say so without collapsing: “That’s a fair point. Let me look at it again.” If not, you can disagree respectfully: “I see it differently, and here is why.” “A soft answer turns away wrath” (Proverbs 15:1). A calm reply is the fruit of security, not weakness.

Clarify without grovelling

If you said something that could be misunderstood, it is often right to clarify, briefly and simply: “I don’t think I put that well. What I meant was …” Then stop. You do not need to apologise repeatedly or explain at length. Jesus taught, “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37). Over-explaining is often the fear of man talking. “When words are many, transgression is not lacking, but whoever restrains his lips is prudent” (Proverbs 10:19).

Apologise when it is right, and only then

If you were wrong or unkind, say so plainly, without excuses. “he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy” (Proverbs 28:13). A Christian can apologise freely, because our worth no longer depends on being right. But do not apologise for things that were not wrong simply to make someone like you again. That is not humility. It is fear.

Sometimes the wise thing is simply to let a slight go. “Good sense makes one slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook an offense” (Proverbs 19:11).

Afterwards: stop the replay

When the conversation keeps playing in your head, do not simply try to stop thinking. Redirect. Paul says, “do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6). Tell God what happened, what you fear, and what you would like. Then turn your mind: “whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, … think about these things” (Philippians 4:8).

Ask what is actually true. Usually the other person has thought about the moment far less than you have. You might write down the fear, and beside it a verse from this study: “There is therefore now no condemnation” (Romans 8:1), or “What can man do to me?” (Psalm 118:6). If there is something to do, such as an email to send or a conversation to have, do it, and then leave it with God.

Speak the truth in love

Freedom from the fear of man does not make us harsh. The goal is “speaking the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15). The question shifts from “How will this make me look?” to “What would serve this person, and honour God?”

Do not walk alone

Tell one or two trusted Christian friends about your struggle. They can help you see clearly, pray for you and remind you of the gospel when your heart forgets.

When fear becomes anxiety

For some people this fear becomes overwhelming: dreading social situations for days, avoiding meetings, panic, sleeplessness or constant worry. This may be social anxiety, which is common and very treatable. Seeing a doctor or a qualified counsellor is not a failure of faith. God often gives help through such means, and medicine, where it is prescribed, is a good gift. The study Contentment & Anxiety and the study Depression & the Christian say more.

If the pain ever leads to thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, please get help now. Call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), and tell someone you trust. Your life is precious to God.

An example

A project manager has a habit of sending long follow-up emails after any tense meeting, explaining herself again and again. She decides to try something different. After the next difficult meeting she pauses, prays, writes one short, honest line of clarification, and closes the laptop. That evening, when the replay begins, she tells God about it and reads Psalm 56. The fear is still there, but it no longer runs her evening.

Further reading

Edward T. Welch’s When People Are Big and God Is Small is a warm, practical book on this subject. Timothy Keller’s short book The Freedom of Self-Forgetfulness, on 1 Corinthians 3 and 4, explores the freedom of living from God’s verdict.

Growth here is slow, and the old fear will return at times. That is not defeat. Each time you turn from people’s verdict to God’s, you are learning to live as what you already are: a beloved child of God, whose life is hidden with Christ.

For reflection

Which of these practices would help you most in the moment, and which afterwards? Is there a misunderstanding you need to clarify, or an apology you need to make, or one you need to stop making? Who could you talk to honestly about your fear of others? What truth from this study will you carry into your next difficult conversation?
